title: Stop putting off the task you keep avoiding
summary: For anyone who keeps delaying an important task. Six steps cover the feeling behind delay, its real cost, what drives it, near deadlines, self-forgiveness and a setup that makes starting easier.

steps.title: Procrastination is a mood problem, not a time problem
steps.body: When you put off a task, you are usually not bad at planning. You are avoiding a feeling, such as boredom, doubt or dread, that the task stirs up. Putting it off brings quick relief, and that relief rewards the habit. So a better calendar alone rarely fixes it. Start by noticing the feeling.
steps.deeper:
Researchers Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl describe procrastination as short-term mood repair: you choose the feel-better option now and hand the cost to your future self. The relief is real, which is why the pattern repeats even when you know it is a bad trade.

Say you keep dodging an email to a client about a mistake. The email itself takes five minutes. What you are really avoiding is the small jolt of embarrassment, so you check messages, tidy your desk or start an easier job instead.

Pick one task you have avoided this week and finish this sentence on paper: I keep putting it off because it makes me feel ___. Naming the feeling is the first move, and the next steps in this journey deal with it.

source.title: Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation: Consequences for future self
source.author: Fuschia M. Sirois and Timothy A. Pychyl

steps.title: Delay buys relief now and sends the bill later
steps.body: Putting things off feels like a win at first. In one classic study of college students, procrastinators had less stress and fewer illnesses early in the term. By the end they had more of both, and their grades were lower. The calm you buy today is borrowed from your future self, with interest.
steps.deeper:
Dianne Tice and Roy Baumeister followed students in a health psychology course across a semester. Early on, those who delayed their work looked better off. Later, as deadlines closed in, they reported higher stress and more illness, and they earned worse results on their work. Delay moved the pain rather than removing it.

Picture two people with a report due in three weeks. One starts with a rough outline on day one and feels a little uneasy. The other spends two weeks feeling fine, then works late for three nights, sleeps badly and hands in something rushed.

Look at the avoided task from the last step and write down two things, what putting it off has cost you so far and what finishing the first small piece would remove from your mind.

source.title: Longitudinal study of procrastination, performance, stress, and health: The costs and benefits of dawdling
source.author: Dianne M. Tice and Roy F. Baumeister

steps.title: Tasks you dislike and that feel far away get delayed most
steps.body: A large review of procrastination research found a pattern. People delay most when a task is unpleasant, when the reward or deadline is far off, when they doubt they can do it, and when they are impulsive. Each of these is something you can change, so look at the task, not at your character.
steps.deeper:
Piers Steel pulled together many studies in a meta-analysis, a combined analysis of earlier research. Task aversiveness, distance from the deadline, low confidence and impulsiveness kept showing up as the main drivers. That means a delay often has a specific cause you can name and shrink.

Writing a tax summary is boring and the due date is months away, so it loses to anything that feels good today. Cleaning the kitchen might feel better because it is concrete and gives a quick win. The kitchen is not more important, it is just closer and clearer.

Take your avoided task and mark which of the four drivers fits best: dull, far away, doubtful or tempting to dodge. Write one change that eases it, such as a first step you can finish in ten minutes.

source.title: The nature of procrastination: A meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure
source.author: Piers Steel

steps.title: Cut a big job into pieces with their own deadlines
steps.body: One deadline at the very end gives you no reason to start today. Several smaller deadlines, spaced across the time you have, give you checkpoints that pull work forward. In a classic study, students with evenly spaced deadlines did better than students whose papers were all due at the end.
steps.deeper:
Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch ran a class with three papers. Students given evenly spaced deadlines did better than those who could hand everything in at the end. Students who chose their own deadlines landed in between. Even deadlines you set yourself helped, though outside ones helped more.

Instead of a report due on the 30th, you set the outline for the 8th, a first draft for the 17th and edits for the 25th. Each date is near enough to feel real, and each piece is small enough to start without dread.

Split the avoided task into three pieces and give each a date. Tell one other person the first date, since a deadline someone else knows about is harder to quietly move.

source.title: Procrastination, deadlines, and performance: Self-control by precommitment
source.author: Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch

steps.title: Forgive yourself for delaying, and you delay less next time
steps.body: Beating yourself up over procrastination feels responsible, but it makes the next round worse. In a study of students, those who forgave themselves for putting off studying for a first exam procrastinated less on the next one. Guilt added to the bad mood that drives avoidance.
steps.deeper:
Michael Wohl, Timothy Pychyl and Shannon Bennett found that self-forgiveness after a first bout of delay was linked to less negative mood and less procrastination before the next exam. Since delay is a way to escape bad feelings, piling shame on top gives you more to escape from.

You meant to write a proposal last week and did not. The harsh thought is that you are lazy. The more useful thought is that last week was busy, the task felt vague, and you can take the first small step now.

When you catch yourself delaying, say one sentence to yourself, such as I put this off and that is done, so what is the next small step. Then do that step for ten minutes.

source.title: I forgive myself, now I can study: How self-forgiveness for procrastinating can reduce future procrastination
source.author: Michael J. A. Wohl, Timothy A. Pychyl and Shannon H. Bennett

steps.title: Make starting easier, sooner and more rewarding
steps.body: You can raise your odds of starting by changing three things about a task. Make the first step easy and clear, attach a reward you care about, and bring the payoff or deadline closer. Cut the temptations that sit within reach. Run this check on one task, then repeat.
steps.deeper:
Piers Steel's procrastination equation sums up the research: motivation rises with confidence and the value of the task, and falls with delay and with how easily you are distracted. Each part can be adjusted. You do not need more willpower if you change the setup.

For a dull expense report you might open the file and enter just the first five receipts, play a favorite playlist only while you do it, set a dated check-in with your manager, and leave your phone in another room.

Choose one avoided task and set it up using the check. Name the tiny first step, add a small reward, set a near deadline and move one distraction out of reach. Then start a ten minute timer.

source.title: The Procrastination Equation: How to Stop Putting Things Off and Start Getting Stuff Done
source.author: Piers Steel
